1.title: ARCHITECTURE GOVERNANCE
1.text: Welcome to Module 12. We've touched on governance throughout this course — in Phase G, in the Architecture Contract, in compliance reviews. Now we bring it all together. Architecture Governance is how architectures are managed and controlled across the whole enterprise: the boards, the frameworks, the compliance processes, and the discipline that keeps an architecture from drifting into irrelevance. The Architecture Board and the levels of conformance are the two topics the exam reliably tests here, so let's make sure both are rock-solid.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's the plan. You'll define Architecture Governance and place it correctly among the broader governance domains. You'll list the six characteristics of governance. You'll describe the Architecture Governance Framework, with its conceptual and organizational structures. You'll explain the Architecture Board — its role, size, and responsibilities. And you'll describe Architecture Compliance and the levels of conformance. Of all of this, prioritize the Architecture Board and the conformance levels — those are the two areas the exam concentrates on, and both reward precise memorization.

1.title: What Is Architecture Governance?
1.text: Let's define it. Architecture Governance is the practice and orientation by which Enterprise Architectures, and other architectures, are managed and controlled at an enterprise-wide level. Notice the standard's emphasis: governance is less about overt control and strict rule-following, and more about guidance and the effective, equitable use of resources to sustain the organization's strategic objectives. And remember a point we established in Module 6 — governance runs continuously across all ADM phases, not just Phase G. So the essence is: governance means managed and controlled, but with a deliberate lean toward guidance rather than rigid enforcement.

1.title: The 4 Governance Domains
1.text: Architecture Governance doesn't stand alone — it operates within a hierarchy of governance domains. At the broadest is Corporate Governance, which is largely beyond the scope of an architecture framework. Within that sits Technology Governance. Within that, IT Governance. And within that, our focus, Architecture Governance. Each of these domains can also exist at multiple geographic levels — global, regional, and local — in a large enterprise. So the nesting to remember runs Corporate, then Technology, then IT, then Architecture. Architecture Governance is the most specific of the four, operating inside the broader governance structures above it.

1.title: The Nature of Governance
1.text: Let's dwell briefly on what governance fundamentally is, because the exam sometimes tests the concept rather than the mechanics. At its core, governance is about ensuring that business is conducted properly. It's built on guidance and accountability rather than pure enforcement. And it provides the structure through which objectives are set and performance is monitored. So if you're asked what governance is really about, the answer isn't "control for its own sake" — it's about doing things properly and sustainably, combining guidance with accountability. That framing will help you reject the overly heavy-handed answer options the exam likes to offer.

1.title: The 6 Characteristics of Governance
1.text: Now a list worth memorizing — the six characteristics of governance. Discipline: a commitment by all parties to adhere to the established procedures, processes, and authority structures. Transparency: all actions and the reasoning behind them are open to inspection by authorized parties. Independence: processes are set up to minimize or avoid conflicts of interest. Accountability: identifiable groups, such as governance boards, are authorized and answerable for their decisions. Responsibility: each party acts responsibly toward the organization and its stakeholders. And Fairness: no decision or process creates unfair advantage for any one party. Six characteristics — Discipline, Transparency, Independence, Accountability, Responsibility, Fairness. The exam often asks "which is NOT one of these?", so know all six.

1.title: The Architecture Governance Framework
1.text: TOGAF gives you a practical Architecture Governance Framework that you can adapt and apply, both for Enterprise Architecture and for other forms of IT architecture. And the key fact to remember is that this framework has two structures. The conceptual structure deals with the processes and the content of governance — how governance actually works on your architecture. The organizational structure deals with the people and bodies that do the governing — who is responsible. Two structures, then: conceptual, which is process and content, and organizational, which is people. Keep them paired in your mind, because the exam may ask you to distinguish them.

1.title: The Conceptual Structure
1.text: Let's look at the conceptual structure — the process side. Here, governance processes act on architecture content, under control, through a managed lifecycle: develop, then implement, then deploy, then monitor. Around that process sits a repository holding three kinds of information: reference data, which is the standards and guidance you govern against; process status, which tracks where things are; and audit information, which records what happened and why. Together these enable compliance, control, and accountability over your architecture. So the conceptual structure, in one line, is the governance process plus the governed content plus the control mechanisms that hold it together.

1.title: The Organizational Structure
1.text: Now the organizational structure — the people side. This defines the bodies, the roles, and the responsibilities for governance. It's centered on the Architecture Board, which we'll come to next, and it's supported by the governance processes and the Architecture Contract. It also links upward and outward to the Corporate, Technology, and IT governance structures we saw in the hierarchy. So where the conceptual structure answered "how does governance work?", the organizational structure answers "who does the governing?" — and the headline answer to that is the Architecture Board. Process versus people, one more time.

1.title: The Architecture Board
1.text: Let's meet the central governance body — the Architecture Board. This is a cross-organization body responsible for the governance and oversight of the architecture. It's typically representative, meaning it includes representatives from all the key stakeholders in the architecture, so that decisions carry broad legitimacy. On size, the standard gives a specific recommendation: four or five permanent members, and no more than ten — kept small deliberately, though membership may rotate over time to maintain enterprise-wide representation. It may operate at the enterprise level, the business-unit level, or both. So for the exam, remember the number: four or five, no more than ten. It's the beating heart of the organizational structure.

1.title: Responsibilities of the Architecture Board
1.text: What does the Architecture Board actually do? Its responsibilities include ensuring consistency between the various sub-architectures, so they fit together coherently. Identifying reusable components, to maximize value. Ensuring the flexibility of the Enterprise Architecture, so it can meet changing business needs and leverage new technology. Enforcing Architecture Compliance. Improving the maturity of the architecture discipline within the organization. And ensuring the discipline of architecture development itself. So in essence, the Board governs, it enforces compliance, and it drives both consistency and reuse across the enterprise. It's not a rubber stamp — it's an active steward of architectural quality.

1.title: Setting Up & Operating the Board
1.text: A word on how the Board is established and run. Setting it up means defining its remit, its size, its structure, and its authority, all within the context of corporate governance. Operating it means regular meetings where the Board reviews and approves architecture work, architecture contracts, and requests for dispensation. And crucially, the Board has genuine decision-making authority within its remit — it can approve, it can enforce, and it can grant dispensations from the standards. So don't think of the Architecture Board as advisory or toothless. It has real authority, and that authority is exactly what lets governance actually bite when projects start to drift.

1.title: Governance & the Architecture Contract
1.text: Let's reconnect to something from Module 6 — the Architecture Contract, signed in Phase G. In the context of governance, the Architecture Contract is a key instrument. It's used to drive architecture change and to ensure conformance between what's built and what was designed. For a contract to actually be effective, the governance framework around it needs certain qualities: simple processes, clear and people-centered authority, strong communication, and a timely, effective escalation process. So the link to hold is this: governance enforces the architecture through the Architecture Contract. The contract is where governance meets delivery and makes conformance contractual rather than merely hoped-for.

1.title: Architecture Compliance
1.text: Now Architecture Compliance, which is an essential part of governance — making sure individual projects actually comply with the Enterprise Architecture. TOGAF describes two complementary processes for this. First, the architecture function prepares Project Architectures: project-specific views of the Enterprise Architecture that show how the EA impacts each major project, drawing on ADM Phases A to F. Second, the governance function defines a formal Architecture Compliance review process for checking the compliance of all projects. So compliance rests on two legs: Project Architectures, which show the EA's impact on a project, and formal compliance reviews, which check that the project lives up to it. Both are needed.

1.title: The 6 Levels of Conformance
1.text: Here's a list the exam genuinely loves — the six levels of architecture conformance, from least to most aligned. Irrelevant: the implementation has no features in common with the architecture at all. Consistent: the features they do have in common are all implemented in accordance with the architecture. Compliant: some common features are in accordance, some features may be missing, but crucially none contradict the architecture. Conformant: all the architecture's features are present in the implementation; some may not be fully in accordance, but again none contradict. Fully Conformant: all features are present and all are in accordance — the gold standard. And Non-Conformant: one or more features actually contradict the architecture. Two anchors to memorize: Non-Conformant means contradicts, and Fully Conformant means all present and all in accordance.

1.title: Conformance — The Key Distinctions
1.text: Let's sharpen the two distinctions students most often trip over. First, compliant versus conformant. Compliant allows features to be missing — what matters is that nothing contradicts. Conformant requires all the architecture's features to be present, even if some aren't fully in accordance, again with nothing contradicting. So conformant is more complete than compliant. Second, Fully Conformant is the strongest positive level — everything present and everything in accordance. And third, the one to never forget: Non-Conformant is the only level that actually contradicts the architecture. The single trigger word that should make you reach for Non-Conformant is "contradicts." If an implementation contradicts the architecture, it's Non-Conformant, full stop.

1.title: Architecture Compliance Reviews
1.text: Let's look at the compliance review itself. An Architecture Compliance review is a formal review of a project against the architecture — its standards, its principles, and its requirements. Its goals are to catch deviations early, while they're cheap to fix; to ensure the agreed standards are actually being applied; and to identify where a project might legitimately need a dispensation. These reviews are conducted by the architecture function under the umbrella of governance. So think of compliance reviews as the early-warning system of governance: they detect deviations early and feed the resulting decisions back into the governance process. Catching drift early is far cheaper than discovering it at go-live.

1.title: Dispensations
1.text: We've mentioned dispensations a few times — let's define one properly. A dispensation grants a time-limited exemption from compliance, with a valid, recorded rationale. It allows a project to proceed in a non-compliant way, but only under controlled, documented conditions, and only for a limited time. And it's granted by the governance body — the Architecture Board. So a dispensation is not a loophole or a permanent escape hatch; it's a governed, temporary exception to the standards, with a clear justification and an expiry. When the exam describes a project being allowed to deviate from the architecture under controlled conditions, that's a dispensation.

1.title: Governance Runs Across the ADM
1.text: Let's reinforce a point that's caught many candidates out. Governance is continuous — it's present in every phase of the ADM, not just Phase G. In fact, the governance framework and the Architecture Board are established right back in the Preliminary Phase, before any architecture cycle begins. Phase G is special only in that it's specifically about implementation governance — governing the build. So the full picture is this: governance is set up in the Preliminary Phase, applied throughout every phase of the ADM, and focused specifically on delivery in Phase G. If a question claims governance happens only in Phase G, that's the trap — it's a continuous, cross-cutting discipline.

1.title: Key Success Factors
1.text: What makes governance actually work in practice? TOGAF highlights several success factors. You need best-practice processes that are clear and simple — convoluted governance gets ignored. You need organizational structures with real authority, which is exactly what the Architecture Board provides. You need a well-managed Architecture Repository, holding your reference data, process status, and audit information. And you need strong communication backed by an effective escalation path, so issues get raised and resolved rather than buried. In short, effective governance rests on four pillars: process, people, repository, and communication. Weaken any one of them and governance starts to lose its grip.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let's clear the traps. One: "governance only happens in Phase G" — no, it's continuous, and it's set up in the Preliminary Phase. Two: "conformant means all features are in accordance" — no, that's Fully Conformant; plain conformant allows some features not in accordance, as long as none contradict. Three: "Non-Conformant just means incomplete" — no, it specifically means the implementation contradicts the architecture. And four: "the Architecture Board has no real authority" — no, it has genuine decision-making authority and grants dispensations. The two things to over-learn are the conformance ladder and the six governance characteristics. Those are the most likely to appear.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Your governance cheat-sheet. There are four governance domains — Corporate, Technology, IT, Architecture. There are six characteristics — Discipline, Transparency, Independence, Accountability, Responsibility, Fairness. The Governance Framework has two structures — conceptual and organizational. The key body is the Architecture Board, with roughly three to ten members. There are six levels of conformance. The strongest positive level is Fully Conformant, and the only contradicting level is Non-Conformant. And a controlled exception is called a dispensation. Capture this card — it holds every number this module is likely to test.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's recap. Architecture Governance manages and controls architectures enterprise-wide, leaning on guidance rather than rigid control. It sits within four domains — Corporate, Technology, IT, and Architecture — and has six characteristics. The Governance Framework has a conceptual structure for process and an organizational structure for people. The Architecture Board is the key governing body, and the Architecture Contract is the key enforcement instrument. And compliance is measured across six levels of conformance, with dispensations providing governed exceptions. Governance is the discipline that keeps everything else honest.

1.title: Memory Hook
1.text: Two memory hooks to lock this in. For the characteristics, remember the string D-T-I-A-R-F: Discipline, Transparency, Independence, Accountability, Responsibility, Fairness. And for conformance, picture a ladder from worst to best: Non-Conformant at the bottom, then Irrelevant, Consistent, Compliant, Conformant, and Fully Conformant at the top. The two trigger phrases that resolve most conformance questions: "contradicts" points to Non-Conformant, and "all present and all in accordance" points to Fully Conformant. D-T-I-A-R-F and the conformance ladder — drill those two and the module's hardest recall is handled.

1.title: Bridge to Module 13
1.text: So where to next? Governance spends a lot of its energy enforcing standards — and TOGAF actually ships two reference models that seed those standards and give architects a head start. Those are the Technical Reference Model and the Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model, and they're the subject of Module 13. The connecting idea is this: reference models provide ready-made starting taxonomies, which governance then adopts and standardizes for the enterprise. Having covered how standards are enforced, we'll next look at where some of those standards come from. On to the reference models.

1.title: Quick Self-Check
1.text: A quick self-check. From memory: can you list the four governance domains and the six characteristics? Can you name the two structures of the Governance Framework? Can you describe the Architecture Board — its nature and rough size? And can you order the levels of conformance and pick out the one that contradicts the architecture? If the conformance levels feel even slightly uncertain, go back and re-watch slides fifteen and sixteen. That conformance ladder is the single most likely thing to be tested from this module, so it's worth the extra minute.

1.title: Why Governance Ties It All Together
1.text: Before the questions, let me underline how central governance is. It's the glue that binds the framework together: it enforces the contracts from Module 6, it applies the standards from the repository in Module 8, and it serves the stakeholders from Module 11. It's what makes an architecture controlled, compliant, and accountable rather than a well-meaning document nobody follows. Without governance, the architecture drifts and quietly loses its value over time. So recognize that governance is continuous and cross-cutting — it reaches into nearly every other module we've covered. That's why it earns its own dedicated lesson here near the end.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question 1. Within which hierarchy of governance domains does Architecture Governance operate? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is A. Corporate, Technology, IT, Architecture Architecture Governance typically operates within a hierarchy of governance domains: Corporate Governance, Technology Governance, IT Governance, and Architecture Governance. The other options are landscape levels, BDAT domains, and stakeholder-management steps.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question 2. Which of the following is NOT one of the six characteristics of governance? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is C. Profitability The six characteristics of governance are Discipline, Transparency, Independence, Accountability, Responsibility, and Fairness. Profitability is not among them.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question 3. In the levels of architecture conformance, which level means that one or more features contradict the architecture? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is D. Non-Conformant Non-Conformant is the level where one or more implemented features contradict the architecture. "Compliant" and "Conformant" mean nothing contradicts (with differing completeness), and "Fully Conformant" means all features are present and all are in accordance.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question 4. What is the primary governance body in TOGAF, and what is its recommended size? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. The Architecture Board, with four or five permanent members (and no more than ten) The Architecture Board is the cross-organization body responsible for governance and oversight of the architecture, representing all key stakeholders. Its recommended size is four or five permanent members, and no more than ten. The other options are not governance bodies.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question 5. What is a dispensation in the context of Architecture Governance? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. A time-limited, governed exemption from compliance granted with valid rationale A dispensation is a time-limited, governed exemption from compliance, granted by the governance body (Architecture Board) with valid rationale. It lets a project proceed non-compliantly under controlled, recorded conditions — it is not a permanent waiver.
